newsitem.title: ICELAND: Iceland puts price tag on sub-glacial flood damage.
newsitem.headline: Iceland puts price tag on sub-glacial flood damage.

text.p: Iceland on Thursday put the estimated damage bill from flooding caused by a sub-glacial volcano at around $16.5 million and scientists warned that more eruptions were possible in the remote area.

The melt flow from a lake in southeastern Iceland under the Vatnajokull icefield, Europe's largest glacier, was returning to normal two days after a torrent of black sulphurous water and debris flooded an uninhabitated plain, media reports said.

Hreinn Haraldsson, director of research and development at the Public Road Administration, said repairing damage caused by the flood would cost an estimated 1.1 billion Icelandic crowns, the equivalent of $16.5 million.

The torrent, pushing hundreds of huge chunks of ice several kilometres, smashed a 400-metre (1,300 foot) steel and concrete bridge over the Gigjukvisl river and damaged a nearby 900-metre (2,950-foot) span over the river Skeidara. It also swept away power lines and parts of the 35-km 22-mile) stretch of Iceland's coastal ring road snaking past the glacier.
Haraldsson said temporary bridges would be built in six to eight weeks to restore traffic on the road, which is used for transporting fish from eastern ports to Reykjavik about six hours away by car.
"It will then take one to two years to rebuild the bridges," he said. "We have not decided yet whether to build them stronger than before."

The bridges were built two decades ago to withstand no more than about 15,000 cubic metres (530,000 cubic feet) per second. At its peak on Tuesday, the water gushed out at 45,000 cubic metres (1.6 million cubic feet) per second.

On Wednesday, a brief volcanic eruption sent clouds of smoke and steam billowing 14,000 (4,300 metres) feet above the glacier. Early last month a series of violent sub-glacial volcanic explosions last month melted water and fed the hidden lake Grimsvotn.
Scientists said more eruptions could follow beneath the glacier, which covers two of Iceland's most active volcanoes.

"For 60 years both these volcanoes have been suspiciously quiet," said Pall Einarsson, a professor of geophysics at the University of Iceland. "But the last year and a half has been a period of unrest. We may see further eruptions somewhere in the glacier in the next few months or years."

Scientists estimated a total of 3,000 billion litres of melted water had amassed in the lake before Tuesday's flood. Einarsson said they were trying to establish how much was left in Grimsvotn, which floods once every five years because of the buildup of meltwater from volcanic and geothermal activity.
Iceland, a volcanic island in the North Atlantic just below the Arctic Circle, is covered to 11 percent by glaciers with the rest mostly mountains and lava fields resembling a moonscape.
The 270,000 citizens, decendants of Viking settlers who arrived more than 1,000 years ago, are used to natural disasters from earthquakes to volcano eruptions.
"You really see the forces of nature at work here, building up and tearing down as well," Einarsson said.
